opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful to separate two things: what pure linear attention does to *efficiency*, and what it does to *intelligence*. The efficiency story is clear. You get linear complexity in sequence length, a fixed-size state, and much cheaper long-context inference. The intelligence story is more subtle.

The core issue is that pure linear attention compresses the entire history into a fixed-size state. Full attention keeps every token around and can go back and look at any of them precisely. That matters a lot for capabilities we care about: exact retrieval, copying, multi-hop reasoning over long documents, and especially long chains of thought in agentic tasks, where the model has to refer back to something specific it saw thousands of steps earlier. A compressed state is inherently lossy, so you tend to see degradation on exactly those retrieval-heavy, precision-heavy tasks, even if perplexity looks fine.

So my view is that pure linear attention, at least in the forms we've seen so far, tends to cap certain kinds of intelligence. It's not that the model becomes "dumb." On a lot of short-context benchmarks it can be quite competitive. But when you push toward long-horizon reasoning, which is where I think the frontier is going, the bottleneck shows up.

That's why the more promising direction, in my opinion, is hybrid architectures. You use linear attention or similar mechanisms for most layers to get efficiency, and keep some full-attention layers, or design better state-update rules, so the model retains precise recall where it needs it. The interesting research question is how far you can push the ratio, and how expressive you can make the recurrent state, without losing capability.

More broadly, I think architecture choices should be judged by one criterion: under a fixed compute budget, do they give you better scaling of intelligence, especially on long-context and agentic tasks? Efficiency matters a lot because it lets you think longer and use more tokens. But if you lose the ability to use those tokens well, you haven't really gained anything. So the goal is to make attention cheaper *without* making the model forget.

r001.rationale: The response says pure linear attention compresses history into a fixed-size, lossy state, which degrades precise retrieval and other tasks. This identifies an architectural constraint as a reason intelligence may be impaired.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that pure linear attention, by itself, costs you intelligence, and we should be clear-eyed about that before talking about how to recover it.

The core issue is that linear attention compresses the entire context into a fixed-size state. No matter how long the sequence is, the model has to squeeze everything into a matrix of fixed dimension. Standard softmax attention doesn't have this constraint; it keeps the full KV cache, so it can go back and retrieve any token precisely. That's why if you look at tasks like needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, or anything that requires exact recall of something that appeared far back in the context, pure linear attention degrades quite noticeably. The information is lossy. It's a bit like asking someone to remember a long document from a summary versus letting them re-read it.

So the question becomes: what is intelligence actually made of? I'd break it into two parts. One is the ability to learn patterns and compress knowledge, which is largely about parameters and training. Linear attention does fine there. The other is in-context retrieval and in-context learning, where the model has to pick out specific pieces of information from what it has just seen and reason over them. That second part is where pure linear attention is weak, and that second part happens to be exactly what matters most for agents, for long-horizon reasoning, for anything where the model is doing real work over a long context.

That's why I'm fairly skeptical of going fully linear. In our own experiments, when we went all the way, the gap showed up most clearly on the hardest, most retrieval-heavy evaluations, and those are the ones that correlate with what users actually feel as "smart."

The more productive framing is a hybrid. You keep a small fraction of full attention layers, and you use linear attention for the rest. Our experience is that you don't need many full attention layers to preserve most of the retrieval capability. The linear layers handle the bulk of local pattern processing efficiently, and the sparse full attention layers act as the precise lookup mechanism. It's not a compromise in the negative sense; it's recognizing that the two mechanisms are good at different things.

The other point I'd make is about scaling behavior. People often compare architectures at a fixed small scale and see linear attention looks competitive. But the gap tends to widen with scale and with longer contexts, because the fixed-size state becomes the bottleneck exactly when you give the model more to remember. So I'd be careful about extrapolating from small-scale ablations.

The upside is that the efficiency gain is real. Decoding cost no longer grows with context length, and that unlocks very long contexts and much cheaper inference. For agent workloads, that matters a lot. So the design problem is how to buy that efficiency while giving up as little of the retrieval capability as possible, and the hybrid approach is currently the best answer I know of.

r001.rationale: The response identifies linear attention’s fixed-size context state as a structural constraint that loses information and weakens retrieval, explaining how the architecture can impair intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is what information the model can retain and retrieve. With pure linear attention, you typically compress the history into a fixed-size state. That makes it efficient, but it also creates a bottleneck: as the context grows, more information has to share the same capacity.

With full attention, the model can go back to individual tokens and decide which ones matter for the current query. That flexibility can be important when a task requires precise recall or combining details from different parts of a long context. So my concern is that pure linear attention may sacrifice some of that ability, even if it performs well on average language-modeling metrics.

But I wouldn’t equate that directly with a fixed ceiling on intelligence. The outcome depends on the architecture, the state size, the training, and the task. I’d want to compare models under matched compute budgets and look specifically at retrieval and reasoning as context length increases. That would tell us much more than a single benchmark score.

r001.rationale: The response attributes possible limitations to a fixed-size state bottleneck and reduced precise recall, but it does not identify architectural bias as the reason.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what information the attention mechanism can preserve. In pure linear attention, you typically compress the history into a fixed-size state. That makes computation more efficient, but it also creates a bottleneck: as the context grows, different pieces of information have to share that state.

With full attention, the model can go back and look at individual tokens based on the current query. That’s useful when you need to retrieve a specific detail or distinguish between several very similar things. Linear attention makes that kind of precise access harder.

But I wouldn’t say linear attention necessarily makes a model less intelligent in every respect. It introduces a different tradeoff, and the effect depends on the architecture, the training, and the task. The important test is whether the efficiency gains let you scale enough to compensate for the information you lose.

r001.rationale: The response identifies pure linear attention’s fixed-size state as an architectural bottleneck that makes precise retrieval harder, which may impair model capabilities.
